description: Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
summary:
Your crew has landed near the Moon's south pole. Sunlight is power, shadows are cold, and a solar storm is on its way. What do you do?

Space Base Commander is a browser game for ages 7–12 where players run a Moon outpost for seven weeks. Every job (checking sunlight, driving to a dark crater, covering the shelter with Moon soil) costs crew time, power, air or crew energy, and outside work adds radiation. Take shelter and you stay safe but explore less. Go out and you might find ice, or pay for it. Curio, a helper robot, guides the first week, and weekly recaps show exactly what changed and why.

Real NASA records ground the story: archived May 2024 solar-storm events from DONKI and radiation measurements from the CRaTER instrument on LRO, clearly labeled. The crew and rules are fictional and simplified. Kids learn the real lesson: where you work decides your power, your risk, and your plan.
details:
What it does and how it works

Space Base Commander is a browser game for ages 7–12. You command a small outpost on the Shackleton Connecting Ridge near the Moon's south pole for seven weekly turns.


Each week you spend limited crew time on Mission, Base or Crew jobs: check the sunlight, fly the hop-drone, drive to a dark crater, clean dusty solar panels, cover the shelter with Moon soil, run the air system, rest.

Every job shows its cost in time, power, air and crew energy before you commit, and outside jobs add radiation. When a storm alarm sounds you face a real choice: take shelter and keep the crew safe, or keep working and pay for it in exposure.

Every job gives an instant result, and at the end of the week a recap shows what changed and why, so players can see their own choices at work. Along the way, a report card collects evidence about the ridge: sunlight, radiation, shelter and possible ice. Ice is something to investigate, not an instant fix, so players work out whether this is a good place for a Moon base, the way scientists would.

The science underneath

Storms are named after real events. Our bundled archive of NASA DONKI space-weather records and CRaTER radiation measurements from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (via NASA OSDR RadLab, May 2024) grounds the radiation story. The game labels what is real, simulated and story. The crew and mission are fictional, the rules are simplified, and radiation points are game points, not astronaut health limits.

Benefits and intended impact

Children see cause and effect instead of memorizing facts. A storm raises risk, shelter protects the crew, and a dusty panel means less power. Our teaching goal is one idea: light is a resource, and where you work decides your power, your cold and your radiation risk. We hope players leave understanding that space missions run on planning, trade-offs and teamwork, and that a "safe" choice usually costs something else. We have not yet measured learning with children. Playtesting is our next step.

Meet the crew (how we ideated)

We started with a retro green-terminal look and a lone commander. Then we asked what a seven-year-old would want to spend seven weeks with, and the answer was a crew. The player is the human commander. They are joined by three specialists with credible backgrounds and overlapping duties, like a real crew: Biscuit the dog (engineer), Mochi the bunny (doctor) and Pebble the cat (geologist and explorer). We renamed them late to match how they look. Curio is the helper robot. He began as a physical rover, then became the on-board AI who teaches, because Mission Control briefs and warns while Curio explains. His name nods to NASA's Curiosity rover, and Bea drew his design by hand. Curio's guidance is written by us, not a live chatbot.

How we built it

We began with a fact registry: every fact shown in the game needs a source and a label. The first prototype was a text-only terminal game with a rules engine and bot players that ran thousands of seeded missions to balance costs. We then cut a 14-day loop to seven weeks, and removed the food meter to keep a single clear teaching goal. We rebuilt the interface three times: a 3D ridge in Three.js, restyled to match the flat clip-art crew; a guided Week 1 with Curio; and a Mission Control briefing each week. The rules engine is deterministic TypeScript, so the same seed gives the same run. The browser interface is JavaScript with Three.js 0.160.0, built and served by Node.js scripts and covered by automated tests.


How we used AI
Codex and Claude were our build partners. They helped with design alternatives, code and debugging, research and text drafting, and some vector and 3D artwork, which the game labels "AI-generated". Bea created the layout wireframe, Curio's design and selected vector art, and we made the design decisions. NASA's data is original and not AI-generated. No language model runs during play, and we used no text-to-image tool for the final artwork. Full credits are at kreipri.github.io/NASA2026-Flux/credits.html.

What is creative about it

It turns a hard planning problem into a story: a small crew, a helper robot, a real place and real storms. It also gives children one clear lesson through play instead of a lecture.

What we considered

Age-appropriate words, honest labelling of real versus simulated, accessibility of the controls, and cutting features (food, Mars, live AI events) rather than shipping too many systems at once.
